reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A form of interstitial lung disease in which granulation tissue plugs fill distal airways and alveoli, formerly termed bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia
Presents subacutely over weeks with cough, breathlessness, fever, and malaise, frequently mislabelled and treated as a non-resolving bacterial pneumonia
Cryptogenic (idiopathic) disease is diagnosed only after excluding secondary organizing pneumonia from infection, drugs, radiation, connective tissue disease, and aspiration
Imaging typically shows patchy, often migratory, peripheral or peribronchial consolidation
Characteristic CT signs include the reverse halo (atoll) sign and areas of ground-glass with consolidation
Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a mixed cellularity and helps exclude infection, while surgical or transbronchial biopsy confirms the organizing pattern
The condition characteristically responds rapidly and often dramatically to systemic corticosteroids
Relapse is common when steroids are reduced or stopped, so a gradual taper is usual
reference.pathophysiology: Organizing pneumonia represents a stereotyped pattern of lung repair following alveolar epithelial injury, in which buds of granulation tissue (fibroblasts and myofibroblasts in a loose connective-tissue matrix, known as Masson bodies) fill the alveolar ducts and surrounding alveoli, often extending into respiratory bronchioles. The underlying architecture is preserved without significant fibrosis, which underlies the potential for reversibility. When no cause is identified the process is termed cryptogenic; identical histology can be provoked by infection, drugs, radiation, connective tissue disease, or inhaled toxins.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary infarction (given the reverse halo sign)
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest to characterise the distribution of consolidation
Bronchoalveolar lavage to exclude infection and eosinophilia
Transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy to confirm the organizing pattern
Connective tissue disease serology and a drug and exposure history
Pulmonary function testing, usually showing a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity
redFlags: A rapidly progressive fulminant variant causing acute respiratory failure
Failure to improve on antibiotics prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Features suggesting an underlying connective tissue disease or vasculitis
Relapse or progression during steroid taper
reference.prognosis: Most patients with cryptogenic disease recover fully with corticosteroids, though relapses during tapering are frequent; a minority have progressive or fibrosing disease, and the rare fulminant form carries significant mortality.
pitfalls: Persisting with repeated antibiotic courses for a presumed pneumonia that is actually organizing pneumonia
Labelling disease cryptogenic without excluding drug, infective, and connective tissue causes
Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse
Misinterpreting migratory infiltrates as treatment failure rather than a feature of the disease
